privacy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy.metaDescription: What this site does with your data: one cookie that remembers your language, a theme saved in your browser, and no analytics at all. Each app has its own policy.

intro.heading: What this page covers
intro.body: Atelier Belli is the portfolio of Ivan Lorenzana, a developer based in Tijuana, Mexico. This site is a handful of static pages: there is no account to create, no form to fill in, no comment box and no newsletter. This policy is about the website itself. Each app we publish has its own policy, and those are linked right below, because a policy that covers a website and four apps at once ends up describing none of them accurately.

apps.heading: Privacy for our apps
apps.intro: If you came here from an App Store listing looking for a specific app, one of these four is the page you want:
apps.note: Each one describes what that app stores, where it stores it, and what (if anything) ever leaves your device.

noCollection.heading: What this site collects: nothing
noCollection.body: No analytics, no advertising, no tracking pixels, no session recording, no A/B testing. There is no sign-up, so there is no list you can end up on, and no server of ours that keeps a record of your visit.

cookie.heading: The one cookie
cookie.body: The site sets a single cookie, named NEXT_LOCALE. It holds one of two values, en or es, and its entire job is to remember whether you are reading the site in English or in Spanish. It is set the first time you arrive, from the language your browser asks for, and again whenever you use the language toggle. It lasts one year, it is limited to this site (SameSite=Lax), and it carries no identifier of any kind. Clearing it simply means the site guesses your language again on your next visit.

theme.heading: Light or dark, remembered in your browser
theme.body: When you switch the site between light and dark, that choice is saved in your browser's local storage under the name ab_theme. It is not a cookie: it stays in your browser and is never attached to a request. Clearing your browser data resets it.

hosting.heading: Hosting and fonts
hosting.body: The site is hosted on AWS Amplify. Like any web host, its servers process the requests needed to deliver a page to you, and that includes your IP address; we do not build reports from it and there is no analytics layer on top of it. Most of the type is served by Google Fonts, so your browser fetches those font files directly from Google's servers, and that request is covered by Google's own privacy policy. The display serif is self-hosted from this site.

privacyRights.heading: Your rights
privacyRights.body: There is very little here to exercise data rights over, because we hold very little. If you want to ask anyway, the routes are on our

children.heading: Children
children.body: This site is not directed at children and collects nothing from anyone, of any age. Each app policy says the same for that app.

changes.heading: Changes to this policy
changes.body: If this policy changes, the date above changes with it, and the current version always lives at this URL.

contact.heading: Contact
contact.body: If you have a question about this policy, or about anything the site or an app does with your data, write to us:
contact.name: Atelier Belli

alisioPrivacy.title: Alisio Privacy Policy
alisioPrivacy.metaDescription: Alisio reads your heart rate on Apple Watch and keeps it on your own devices. No account, no analytics, and no networking code anywhere in the app.
alisioPrivacy.intro: Alisio reads your heart rate on your Apple Watch while you train and keeps everything it learns on your own devices. There is no account, no analytics, and no networking code anywhere in the app. Here it is in detail:

collect.heading: What we collect: nothing
collect.body: Alisio has no accounts, no analytics, no ads, no trackers, and no servers of ours. The app contains no networking code at all, so there is no path for anything to leave your devices, and there is no third-party SDK riding along inside it.

health.heading: Health data
health.body: On your Apple Watch, Alisio asks Apple Health for permission to read your heart rate and your active energy while a session is running, and to save the finished workout back into Health. Those readings drive the live zone on your wrist and the summary you get at the end. We never use health data for advertising, never share it with third parties, and never sell it. The iPhone app asks for no permissions at all.
health.prompts: The permission sheets show the app's own words, in Spanish: "Necesitamos tu ritmo cardiaco para calcular tus zonas de entrenamiento." (we need your heart rate to calculate your training zones) and "Guardamos tu entrenamiento en Salud." (we save your workout in Health).

storage.heading: Where your data lives
storage.body: The profile you enter (your age, your resting heart rate, and the formula you pick) is saved in the app's own preferences on your iPhone. Your session history is a plain file inside the app's private folder on that same iPhone. Nothing is copied to iCloud and nothing is copied to us.

devices.heading: Between your Watch and your iPhone
devices.body: Alisio sends your profile to the Watch and the finished session back to the iPhone over Apple's Watch Connectivity, a direct link between two devices you already own. The watch face complication reads a small snapshot that the Watch app leaves in a shared container on the Watch itself. None of that passes through a server of ours, because there is no server of ours.

account.heading: No account, no purchases, no ads
account.body: Alisio has no sign-in, no subscription, no in-app purchases, and no advertising. Every part of it works in airplane mode, indefinitely.

deletion.heading: Deleting your data
deletion.body: Deleting the app removes your profile and your session history from your iPhone. Workouts that Alisio already saved into Apple Health belong to Health and stay there; you can delete those from the Health app, in the section that lists the apps that wrote data.

children.heading: Children
children.body: Alisio collects no data from anyone, including children.

changes.heading: Changes
changes.body: If this policy ever changes, the date above changes with it, and the current version will always live at this URL.

favePrivacy.title: Fave Privacy Policy
favePrivacy.metaDescription: Fave keeps your rankings on your device and in your own iCloud, with no servers of ours in between. What that means for artwork, notes, and deleting the app.
favePrivacy.intro: Fave keeps your rankings on your device and in your personal iCloud account. That is the whole story, but here it is in detail:

collect.heading: What we collect: nothing
collect.body: Fave has no accounts, no analytics, no ads, no tracking, and no servers of our own. We never see your data.

dataLocation.heading: Where your data lives
dataLocation.body: Everything you write in Fave (your lists, entries, ratings, notes, and photos) is stored on your device and synced through your private iCloud database, which only your Apple ID can access. Apple's handling of iCloud data is described in Apple's own privacy policy. Deleting the app and its iCloud data removes everything; we keep no copies, because we never had any.

artwork.heading: Movie, show, and book artwork
artwork.tmdb: When you search for a movie or show, Fave queries The Movie Database (TMDB) and loads poster images from TMDB's servers. Those requests go directly from your device to TMDB and are subject to TMDB's privacy policy. Fave sends only your search text and standard network information; it never sends your rankings, notes, or photos to TMDB or anyone else.
artwork.openLibrary: When you search for a book, Fave queries Open Library and loads cover images from Open Library's servers. Those requests go directly from your device to Open Library and are subject to Open Library's privacy policy. Here too, Fave sends only your search text and standard network information; your rankings, notes, and photos never leave your device and your iCloud account.

children.heading: Children
children.body: Fave collects no data from anyone, including children.

changes.heading: Changes
changes.body: If this policy ever changes, the date above changes with it and the current version will always live at this URL.

fingoPrivacy.title: Fingo Privacy Policy
fingoPrivacy.metaDescription: Fingo picks for you: a finger, a wheel, a number, a coin. It asks for no permissions, has no account, and never connects to anything. Here is the full policy.
fingoPrivacy.intro: Fingo picks for you: a finger, a wheel, a number, a coin. It asks for no permissions, has no account, and never connects to anything. Here it is in detail:

collect.heading: What we collect: nothing
collect.body: Fingo has no accounts, no analytics, no ads, no trackers, and no servers of ours. There is nothing to opt out of, because nothing is being collected in the first place.

storage.heading: Where your data lives
storage.body: Whatever you set up in the app (the wheels you build and the options you type into them, plus your settings for Chooser, Random and Coin Flip) is saved in the app's own preferences on your iPhone. It stays there, and deleting the app takes it with it.

permissions.heading: Permissions: none
permissions.body: Fingo asks for nothing. No camera, no photos, no contacts, no location, no notifications. If iOS ever shows you a permission sheet with Fingo's name on it, something is wrong and we would like to hear about it.

network.heading: Nothing to send, nowhere to send it
network.body: The app contains no networking code and no third-party SDKs. It behaves exactly the same in airplane mode as it does online, because it never had a reason to go online.

children.heading: Children
children.body: Fingo collects no data from anyone, including children.

changes.heading: Changes
changes.body: If this policy ever changes, the date above changes with it, and the current version will always live at this URL.

savelyPrivacy.title: Savely Privacy Policy
savelyPrivacy.metaDescription: Savely tracks your money on your phone and nowhere else. What it stores, the two permissions it asks for, and why receipts never open your photo library.
savelyPrivacy.intro: Savely tracks your money on your phone and nowhere else. The app says so in its own settings: "Your data never leaves this iPhone." Here is what that means in detail:

collect.heading: What we collect: nothing
collect.body: Savely has no account, no sign-in, no analytics, no ads, no trackers, and no servers of ours. It does not sync to iCloud either. We never see a single number you enter.

storage.heading: Where your data lives
storage.body: Your income, your expenses, your goals, and the deposits you make toward those goals are stored in a database inside the app on your iPhone. Your display name and your reminder settings live in the app's own preferences. All of it stays on that phone.

receipts.heading: Scanning a receipt
receipts.body: Savely asks for the camera the first time you scan a receipt, with these words: "Savely uses the camera to scan receipts for recording and managing your expenses." The photo is read on your device by Apple's own text recognition, and the app keeps only the amount, date and description you confirm on the review screen. The image itself is never saved by the app and never uploaded. You can also pick a photo you already have through Apple's photo picker, which hands Savely the single image you chose, so the app never gets access to your photo library.

reminders.heading: Reminders
reminders.body: The reminders are local notifications: your iPhone schedules them and your iPhone shows them. Savely asks for notification permission the first time you open it, and you can turn the reminders off in the app or in iOS Settings. Nothing is pushed from a server, because there is no server.

network.heading: What leaves your phone
network.body: Nothing, unless you send it yourself. The app makes no network requests. The one thing that can travel is the weekly PDF report: it is built on your phone from the current week and handed to the iOS share sheet, and where it goes from there is entirely your decision.

deletion.heading: Deleting your data
deletion.body: "Delete all data", in the Data and privacy section of your profile, removes your income, expenses and goals from the phone. Your name and your reminder settings stay, because they are preferences rather than data. Deleting the app removes everything, those included.

children.heading: Children
children.body: Savely collects no data from anyone, including children.

changes.heading: Changes
changes.body: If this policy ever changes, the date above changes with it, and the current version will always live at this URL. If a future version of Savely ever sends anything off your phone, this page will say so before that version ships.

privacyChoices.title: User Privacy Choices
privacyChoices.metaDescription: How to exercise your data rights with Atelier Belli, and the honest reason answers are short: there is almost nothing here to hand over, correct, or delete.
privacyChoices.intro: Privacy policies usually promise machinery for exercising your data rights. Here is the honest version: we hold almost nothing about you, so for most requests the answer is that there is nothing to hand over, correct, or delete. This page says where the data actually is and how to reach a person about it.

whatWeHold.heading: What we hold about you
whatWeHold.body: Nothing that identifies you. This website has no accounts, no forms and no analytics; it stores a language cookie and a theme preference, both of which live on your own device and neither of which carries an identifier. If you have written to us, we have your email in an inbox, the same way anyone has the email they were sent.

appData.heading: Data inside our apps
appData.body: What our apps hold stays on your device, and in Fave's case in your own iCloud account. We keep no copy and have no way to reach it, so asking us to delete it would not accomplish anything, but you can delete it yourself: each app policy explains exactly what it stores and how to remove it.

requests.heading: Making a request
requests.body: You can still ask us for a copy of anything we hold, ask us to correct it, or ask us to delete it. Given everything above, the answer is usually short and quick.

howToExercise.heading: How to reach us
howToExercise.name: Atelier Belli
howToExercise.responseNote: A person reads that inbox and answers, usually within a few days. We will not ask you for extra personal information to verify a request unless answering it genuinely requires it.
howToExercise.disclaimer: This page describes how we handle requests in practice. It is not a summary of any particular country's data-protection law, and where such a law gives you more than this page does, that law wins.

savely.name: Savely
savely.metaDescription: Help with Savely: totals that read wrong, goals that will not budge, reminders that never arrive. Answers from the person who built the app.

hero.lede: Savely keeps your money on your phone and nowhere else. If a total reads wrong, a goal will not budge, or a reminder never arrives, write in. Every message is read by the person who built the app.

contact.sub: There is no account to look up and no server to check, so the quickest route is simply telling us what you saw.

email.label: Email
email.hint: The main desk. Write any time.

bug.label: Report a bug
bug.hint: What you tapped, what happened, a screenshot if you have one.

feature.label: Request a feature
feature.hint: Savely is version 1.0. A lot is still open.

security.label: Security concern
security.hint: Tell us privately first, so it is fixed before it is public.

faq.sub: The ones that come up most. If yours is not here, just write.

items.q: Where does my money data live?
items.aHtml: On this iPhone, in a private store only Savely can open. There is no account, no cloud copy, and no connection to anything outside the phone. The app says so itself under Me → Data & privacy: your data never leaves this iPhone. The camera is the only permission it ever asks for, and that is for reading receipts.

items.q: If I lose my phone, can I get my data back?
items.aHtml: Not from us, and we would rather be blunt about it. Nothing is ever uploaded, so there is no copy on our side to restore and no account to recover. What does protect you is your iPhone's own backup: Savely stores everything in the app's normal storage, so it travels with an iCloud or computer backup and returns when you restore a phone. That is the honest trade for keeping your finances off the internet.

items.q: How does the receipt scanner work?
items.aHtml: Point the camera at a receipt and iOS reads it on the device, in Spanish or in English. Nothing is uploaded, and the photo itself is never saved. What you get back is a draft: the amount, the merchant, the date and the category are all editable, and nothing is recorded until you tap Save. You can also pick an existing photo from your library instead.

items.q: What does Auto-move on payday actually do?
items.aHtml: Less than the name promises, and you should know that before you rely on it. Nothing moves on a schedule and nothing runs in the background. You switch it on for a goal, and then, when you log income, Savely may offer to move one amount into that goal. It happens only if you say yes, and the deposit is written together with that income.

items.q: Can I export my data, or erase it?
items.aHtml: There is one export, the Weekly PDF report row under Me → Data & privacy. It covers the current week of income and expenses and hands you a PDF through the share sheet, so treat it as something to read rather than a backup to restore from. To erase, use Delete all data in the same place: every income, expense and goal is removed from this iPhone, your name and reminder settings stay, and it cannot be undone.

cta.sub: Write to us directly. Real replies, patient answers.
cta.label: ivanlorenzana@outlook.com

fingo.name: Fingo
fingo.metaDescription: Help with Fingo, the app for settling who pays and who goes first. Answers about its four modes, and a real person who reads every message you send.

hero.lede: Fingo is a small app for settling who pays, who goes first, who picks the music. It runs entirely on your phone, with no account and no internet. If something misbehaves, write to us. A real person reads every message.

contact.sub: Three ways in, all of them landing on the same desk.

email.label: Email
email.hint: The main desk. Write any time.

bug.label: Report a bug
bug.hint: A short note and a screenshot go a long way.

feature.label: Request a feature
feature.hint: We read all of them. Some ship.

faq.sub: The ones that come up most. If yours is not here, just write.

items.q: Does Fingo need an account, or the internet?
items.aHtml: Neither. There is no sign-in and no networking code in the app at all, so it behaves exactly the same in airplane mode. It asks for no permissions, collects nothing, and your wheels are saved only on the phone. Delete the app and nothing is left behind.

items.q: What can Fingo actually decide?
items.aHtml: Four things, one per tab. Chooser picks a finger: everyone holds the screen, and with two or more fingers down a short countdown runs before one is chosen, up to five at a time. Roulette spins a wheel you built yourself. Random gives you a number inside a range you set. Coin Flip is heads or tails.

items.q: I deleted a roulette and it came back. Why?
items.aHtml: So the tab is never empty. If you delete every wheel, Fingo puts the starter one back the next time you open the app: My First Roulette, with the options Yes, No and Maybe. Edit it into something you actually want and it will stay that way.

items.q: Can I turn the vibration off?
items.aHtml: Not inside Fingo today. The app has no settings screen at all, so haptics stay on wherever they fire. If you want a switch for it, write to us and say so.

items.q: Can I save or share a result?
items.aHtml: No, and nothing is kept. A roulette winner appears in a card you dismiss by tapping the background around it, the Chooser clears its result after a moment, and no mode keeps a history. Fingo is built to settle the moment and then get out of the way.

fave.name: Fave
fave.metaDescription: Help with Fave: lists that will not sync, artwork that loads wrong, and how to reach a person. Every message is read by the developer who built the app.

hero.lede: Fave is the notebook for everything you try, and it keeps your lists in your own iCloud rather than on our servers. If a poster loads wrong, a list will not sync, or something simply confuses you, write to us.

contact.sub: There is no account for us to look up, so tell us what you saw and where you saw it.

email.label: Email
email.hint: The main desk. Write any time.

sync.label: iCloud and syncing
sync.hint: Tell us what Profile → Your data shows.

artwork.label: Artwork or titles
artwork.hint: Films and shows come from TMDB, books from Open Library.

bug.label: Report a bug
bug.hint: What you tapped, what happened, a screenshot if you have one.

faq.sub: The ones that come up most. If yours is not here, just write.

items.q: Do I need an account?
items.aHtml: Not with us. Fave has no sign-up, no password and no profile to fill in. Your lists are kept on your iPhone and mirrored to your own private iCloud, so they follow you to a new phone without us ever holding a copy. We cannot read them, and there is nothing on our side to log into.

items.q: What if I am not signed into iCloud?
items.aHtml: Fave still works, it simply cannot carry anything across. Profile → Your data tells you which situation you are in: when there is no iCloud account on the phone it says your lists live only there, and that signing in from Settings will let them keep themselves. Nothing is lost in the meantime.

items.q: What does Fave send to the internet?
items.aHtml: Only what it needs to put a name and a cover on something. Searching a film or a show sends that text to TMDB along with your language setting; searching a book sends the title or the ISBN to Open Library. Posters and covers are downloaded from those same two services, and Fave will quietly fetch a missing one when you open the app. Your stars, your reactions, your notes and your photos are never sent to either of them.

items.q: How do I delete everything?
items.aHtml: In two steps, because there are two copies. Deleting the app clears it from that iPhone, but the synced copy stays in your iCloud and would return if you reinstalled. To remove it for good, delete the app and then delete Fave's iCloud data from your iPhone's Settings. Inside the app you can also delete a single list or entry by holding it down, which removes it from all of your devices.

items.q: Can I rank anything, or only films and books?
items.aHtml: Both. Movies, Shows and Books are built in, with a search that fills in the title, the year and the artwork. Everything else goes in lists you make yourself, which come in two kinds: Things for anything you try, and Places for cafés and venues, where a place is scored by the orders you rate inside it. Every entry can take one to five stars, an emoji, a note and one photo, and all four are optional.

cta.sub: Write to us directly. Real replies, patient answers.
cta.label: ivanlorenzana@outlook.com

alisio.name: Alisio
alisio.metaDescription: Help with Alisio: a Start on Apple Watch button that stays grey, a heart rate stuck at zero, and how your zones are worked out. Every message is read by the developer who built the app.

hero.lede: Alisio reads your heart rate on your Apple Watch and taps your wrist when you enter or leave your zone. Your iPhone sets it up and mirrors it live. If the two stop talking, a number looks wrong, or something simply confuses you, write to us.

contact.sub: There is no account for us to look up, so tell us what you saw, on which device, and what you tapped.

email.label: Email
email.hint: The main desk. Write any time.

sync.label: iPhone and Watch
sync.hint: Tell us which screen you were on and what each device showed.

feature.label: Ideas
feature.hint: The way you train, and what would make it easier.

bug.label: Report a bug
bug.hint: What you tapped, what happened, a screenshot if you have one.

faq.sub: The ones that come up most. If yours is not here, just write.

items.q: Why is Start on Apple Watch grey?
items.aHtml: Because Alisio is not installed on your Watch yet, and the Train tab says so right under the button: Install Alisio on your Apple Watch to start. Open the Watch app on your iPhone, go to Available Apps and install Alisio. The button turns your zone's colour on its own once it is there. If the button is lit but the session does not start, the Watch is usually asleep or Alisio is closed on it: open Alisio on your Watch and tap the button again.

items.q: My heart rate stays at zero. What now?
items.aHtml: It means the Watch is not getting readings. The first time you start a session, the Watch asks Apple Health for permission to read your heart rate and active energy and to save the workout. If that was declined, open the Health app on your iPhone, tap your profile picture, then Apps, pick Alisio and turn those on. On the iPhone, No data from your watch. Is Alisio still open there? means the Watch has stopped sending: raise your wrist and check that Alisio is still running.

items.q: How are my zones worked out?
items.aHtml: From two numbers you set once, in Settings: your age and your resting heart rate. Your age estimates your maximum heart rate with the Tanaka formula (208 minus 0.7 times your age). Karvonen then spreads the five zones across the gap between your resting and your maximum, so your fitness counts; Simple takes plain percentages of the maximum and needs only your age. Zone 1 starts at 50% and each zone is ten points wide, up to 100% in Zone 5. Change either number and Your zones recalculates on the spot and is sent to your Watch.

items.q: Can I train without my iPhone?
items.aHtml: Yes. Open Alisio on your Watch, turn the Digital Crown to pick a zone and tap Start. It remembers the zone you used last. A session started from the Watch has no time goal: the clock runs free and the zone taps work the same. The Watch needs your profile first, so open Alisio on your iPhone once before you head out. When you finish, the session reaches your History as soon as your iPhone is nearby again.

items.q: Do I need an account, and where is my data?
items.aHtml: No account, no sign-in, nothing to pay for inside the app. Your profile and your session history live on your iPhone; the Watch gets a copy of your profile directly from it. Nothing goes to iCloud and nothing goes to us. The finished workout is also saved in Apple Health, and stays there as a regular workout.

items.q: How do I delete a session, or everything?
items.aHtml: To remove one session, open it in History, tap the trash icon and confirm. Deleting the app removes your profile and your whole history from your iPhone. The workouts Alisio already saved in Apple Health belong to Health and stay there; delete those from the Health app.

cta.sub: Write to us directly. Real replies, patient answers.
cta.label: ivanlorenzana@outlook.com

hero.subtitle: A small <it>atelier</it> for software out of Tijuana. Minimalist form, and the patience to finish things. I design and build iOS apps and the web around them.

workbench.desc: A small, opinionated set. Swift and SwiftUI for the phone; <it>Next.js</it> and TypeScript for the web; Postgres for things that must last. Figma, Xcode, Claude Code. The bench stays tidy.

fingo.descRich: For the table that cannot decide who pays or where to eat. Everyone puts a finger on the screen and Fingo picks one; or spin a wheel of your own options, pick a random number, flip a coin. Each pick lands with a <it>haptic thump</it> instead of a sound. Offline, no account, no ads.
fingo.tag: Fingers on the glass, and one gets picked.

savely.descRich: A savings app for people who do not want to hand over their bank login. Set goals and see an honest pace, log income and spending in seconds, and scan receipts that are read right on the phone. On payday it can offer one move into a goal, capped by what the month can afford. No account, no cloud, no bank connection: your money data <it>never leaves the phone</it>.
savely.tag: Savings goals that tell the truth. Money that never leaves your phone.
savely.galleryCaption: Three real screens: a goal with its pace, a receipt read on the phone (the photo is never saved), and the payday move into that goal.

story.problem: Most savings apps want a bank connection before they are useful, then answer the only question that matters, whether the goal still lands on time, with a projection your deposits do not support.
story.approach: Everything runs on the phone: SwiftData for the money, Apple's on-device text recognition for receipts, and no network requests. The pace math refuses to flatter: it uses your last four weeks of deposits, and a goal more than a year out reads 1+ year instead of an invented date. The rebuild got there by removing things: accounts, the cloud and the AI tips all came out.
story.result: Live on the App Store with the premise intact: no account, no cloud, no bank connection. The one thing that can leave the phone is a weekly PDF you share yourself.

highlights: No account, no cloud, no bank connection, no network requests
Receipts read on device by Apple's text recognition; the photo is never saved
The payday move offers one deposit, capped by what the month can afford
Pace from your last four weeks of deposits; past a year it says 1+ year, never a made-up date

mezcal.descRich: The website for Destilería Lorenzana, a family mezcal made in San Bartolo Yautepec, Oaxaca. It tells the founder's story in chapters, walks through the six steps from earth oven to <it>copper still</it>, and presents three agaves by their names, for buyers and distributors who want to know where the bottle comes from.
mezcal.tag: A family mezcal brand: its story, its process, three agaves.
mezcal.titleIt: from a palenque in the Sierra Sur.

briefmark.descRich: For people who save recipes, movies and restaurants from short videos and never find them again. Paste a TikTok or Instagram Reel link and Briefmark hears the audio, reads the frames and hands back tidy cards: the recipe with its ingredients and steps, the movie with <it>where it streams</it> in Mexico, the place with its map. A prototype, paused since May 2026.
briefmark.tag: TikToks and Reels, turned into cards you can act on.

stampi.titleIt: the stamp card that never gets lost.
stampi.descRich: Digital stamp cards for cafés and small shops. A customer scans a QR once and the card saves to Apple Wallet or Google Wallet: no app, no sign-up, no email. Staff stamp it from their own phone, and the card updates itself on the lock screen. Designed, built and run by one person, <it>end to end</it>.
stampi.tag: Loyalty cards that live in Apple and Google Wallet.

story.problem: Paper stamp cards get lost in wallets and washing machines, and a loyalty app is one more download nobody makes. Every customer already carries a wallet on their phone. The card just has to live there and stay current.
story.approach: One platform that speaks both wallets: signed Apple passes kept fresh through Apple's pass web service and silent push, the Google Wallet API, and PIN-protected panels for the counter, the owner and the operator. A wallet outage never blocks a sign-up or a stamp.
story.result: Live at stampi.atelierbelli.com and open to businesses. A stamp at the counter reaches the customer's card moments later without them opening anything, and a finished card arrives as a notice on the lock screen.

highlights: One scan to join: no app, no account, no email
Keeps stamping through an internet outage, then syncs
A scratched QR still works: an 8-character code is printed under it
Up to three lock-screen messages a day to your customers
A wallet failure never blocks a sign-up or a stamp

alisio.titleIt: feel your zone, don't watch it.
alisio.descRich: For anyone who trains by heart rate. Pick a zone and a time; your Apple Watch taps your wrist the moment you drift out and again when you are back, so the workout is something you <it>feel</it>, not a screen you study mid-set. The goal counts only the time you spend in the zone, every workout is saved to Apple Health, and there is no account.
alisio.tag: Your watch taps your wrist when you leave your heart-rate zone.

story.problem: Training by zone means checking your wrist mid-set. At that pace the number arrives late, and looking for it breaks the effort you were trying to hold.
story.approach: The Watch measures and taps, with a different pattern for entering the zone, leaving it and reaching the goal, and only when the state changes. The iPhone mirrors what the Watch tracks. Zones come from your own age and resting heart rate, with maximum heart rate from Tanaka's formula instead of the usual 220 minus age.
story.result: Live on the App Store. Pick a zone and a time and the rest arrives on your wrist; the goal clock pauses whenever you drift out. A watch-face complication shows your zone and BPM without opening the app.

highlights: Three distinct taps: into the zone, out of it, goal reached
The goal clock counts only time spent in the zone
Start from the Watch alone: turn the crown to a zone and go
Your profile reaches the Watch; sessions land in your iPhone history and Apple Health
No account and no server: nothing leaves your devices
alisio.mediaCaption: One live session across both devices: started on the iPhone, measured on the Watch, mirrored back to the phone. Watch the badge flip as the heart rate drifts out of Zone 2 and returns.
alisio.watchCaption: On the wrist: pick a zone with the crown, then the live session slipping out of zone and back in, through to the goal ring closing.

fave.descRich: A notebook for anyone who keeps lists of every drink, café, movie and book they have tried. Tick things off as you go and give stars <it>only when you feel like it</it>, because rating is never homework. A café scores itself from the orders you rated there, and movies and books bring their own covers, in your language's edition. Your lists live in your private iCloud: no accounts, no analytics.
fave.tag: Rank the drinks, cafés, movies and books you try.

vitapath.titleIt: from SOS to hospital, in one system.
vitapath.descRich: An emergency response system for patients with serious conditions. One tap on SOS offers the case to the nearest available paramedics, and the first to accept is tracked live on the real road route. The patient is routed to a hospital their <it>insurance covers</it> and that can treat them, while the hospital console runs dispatch, arrival and reception.
vitapath.tag: One tap sends a paramedic and picks the right hospital.

story.problem: In an emergency the minutes go to deciding who responds and where the patient is taken. Send them to a hospital that does not take their insurance, or cannot handle the case, and the transfer happens twice.
story.approach: One emergency state machine inside database transactions, so exactly one paramedic wins the offer. PostGIS finds the nearest five within 5 km and widens the search every 30 seconds, STOMP keeps the map and ETA live on all three surfaces, and hospital routing weighs insurance, distance and capability with real driving times.
story.result: A working system across two SwiftUI apps, a React console and a Spring Boot backend, behind 338 unit tests. Adding triage once sent a public-insurance patient to a private hospital 340 m away instead of a public one at 730 m; the routing now prefers public hospitals for public coverage.

highlights: Offers widen from 5 km to 25 km until someone accepts
Exactly one paramedic can win an emergency, enforced in the database
Hospital routing by insurance, distance and capability
Each hospital sees only its own patients, with a PHI access audit trail
vitapath.mediaCaption: One emergency, run live through all three surfaces at once. The offer lands on the paramedic's phone, the paramedic accepts, and the console resolves the hospital by insurance and network while the patient watches the same road route close in.
vitapath.galleryCaption: The patient app: the SOS button, live tracking with the paramedic's real road route and ETA, and the emergency card responders read on arrival.

arrhythmia.titleIt: read the ECG, beat by beat.
arrhythmia.descRich: Upload a heart recording and see every detected heartbeat labelled normal or one of four abnormal types, with how sure the model is. The rebuild found that the original's 98% came from mixing patients between training and testing; measured honestly on patients it never saw, it scores <it>63.22%</it>. A research tool, not a medical device.
arrhythmia.tag: Upload an ECG and see every heartbeat classified.

story.problem: The original was a desktop app that plotted the first four seconds of a record and classified one beat per button press. Worse, it evaluated by mixing patients across the split, which inflated every number it reported.
story.approach: One shared pipeline for training and the live API, a beat detector that no longer caps out at 86 bpm, and the inter-patient evaluation protocol from the research literature. A class with only two real training examples was left honest instead of padded with 38,000 synthetic ones.
story.result: A working demo: upload a record and read the whole trace at once, every beat classified with its confidence. 63.22% on 49,687 beats from held-out patients, 168 backend tests, and both repositories are public.

highlights: 5 AAMI classes (N/S/V/F/Q) with per-beat confidence
Evaluated on patients the model never saw: an honest 63% over a leaky 98%
The full 30-minute record, not a four-second slice
One versioned model shared by training and the API
arrhythmia.mediaCaption: MIT-BIH record 230: 2,464 beats, 123 flagged, classified against the live model.
arrhythmia.galleryCaption: Uploading the record, and a flagged beat opened in its real 60-second context window.

jugo.descRich: A free Mac app so your battery never catches you out. Alerts grow out of the notch like a <it>Dynamic Island</it>, macOS's own low-battery pop-up is closed for you since Jugo already said it, and your AirPods, iPhone and mouse sit in one place, down to your iPhone's battery wear and 30 days of which apps drained the Mac.
jugo.tag: Battery alerts that grow out of your Mac's notch.

reel.lede: Six products live this year, each in the cut of its own launch film. Tap one to open its case.

meta.title: Jugo: battery alerts for your Mac
meta.description: Jugo turns your Mac's notch into a Dynamic Island for battery alerts and keeps an eye on your AirPods, iPhone and accessories. Free for macOS.

hero.lede: Jugo turns the notch into a small island that tells you what your battery is doing, right when it matters: when you plug in, when it's full, and before it runs out.
hero.downloadMeta: Version 1.0 · macOS 26 or later · Apple silicon and Intel · 2.5 MB · Notarized by Apple

demo.caption: The island, live: charging, full, and the one you don't want to miss.
demo.aria: Animated example of Jugo alerts growing out of a MacBook notch

film.caption: Twenty seconds of Jugo. Sound on.

devices.body: Open Jugo from the menu bar and see your Mac next to your AirPods (left, right and case), your iPhone and iPad over USB or Wi‑Fi, and your Magic accessories. Lowest first, so whatever needs a charger is always on top.
devices.caption: The menu, captured on a real Mac.
devices.alt: Jugo's menu: the Mac at 82% with 7 h 40 min left and 96% health, battery stats, and AirPods Pro at 100%

health.body: The numbers macOS keeps to itself, in plain view. These are from the Mac in the capture above.
stats: Capacity today versus new, the same figure System Settings shows.
How much of its rated life the battery has used so far.
Real capacity, not just a percentage.
What's going in or coming out, right now.

items: Alerts you shape: pick the percentage, the sound, the color, and whether it grows from the notch or floats mid-screen.
Knows who's draining it: energy by app for the last hour, day, week or month.
Respects macOS: it follows your charge limit, shows Low Power Mode in yellow like iPhone, and can close the system's own low battery pop-up.
A desktop widget in three sizes, lowest battery first.
Reduce Motion aware: with it on, the island simply fades in and out.
In English and Spanish, following your Mac.

privacy.title: It stays on your Mac.
privacy.body: No account, no analytics, no tracking. Jugo reads your batteries locally. The only thing it ever asks the internet is whether there's a new version.

faq.title: Questions
items: Why isn't it on the Mac App Store?
Reading AirPods, iPhone and per-app energy needs system access the App Store sandbox doesn't allow. Jugo is notarized by Apple instead, and it updates itself.
Yes. No trial, no account, no in-app purchases.
Does my iPhone need a cable?
Only once. Connect it, tap Trust, then turn on “Show this iPhone when on Wi‑Fi” in Finder. From then on Jugo reads it over your network.
A Mac running macOS 26 or later, with Apple silicon or Intel.
